summary.text: 弟 is used chiefly for a younger brother and more broadly for a junior. Early forms are interpreted as a binding wrapped around a shaft or peg; the image-to-meaning account is plausible but not visually confirmed here.

formation.text: Pictographic: the proposed original graph depicts a cord or leather binding wound around an implement. The interpretation is supported as a scholarly reading of early forms, but the implement’s identity and the graphic reading have not been independently verified from inspected images. The proposal that orderly binding led to the sense ‘younger’ is an interpretation, not a securely dated semantic sequence.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a binding wrapped around an implement, variously described as a shaft or peg. Early forms are reported with an element identified as 必/柲, while some bronze forms are described with 弋; the evidence does not establish one as the ancestor of the other. This is a whole-picture analysis, not a demonstrated split into current components.

history.text: The dossier reports oracle-bone and bronze forms, but provides no visually inspected glyphs and establishes no continuous graphic sequence to the modern form. The Shuowen account describes successive leather bindings and says the graph follows an ancient form; this remains a historical lexicographic interpretation.
A later graph, 第, uses 弟 as a phonetic component; that relationship belongs to 第 and does not make 弟 itself phonosemantic.

uncertainties.text: The proposed implement is variously identified as a weapon shaft, peg, or an element related to 柲. Its spoken name is not established, so the dossier cannot demonstrate that the character was borrowed for ‘younger brother’ because the depicted object’s name sounded similar.

The reported early forms do not by themselves establish an early ‘younger brother’ use. The cited Western Zhou bronze inscription contains 弟 in 兄弟, but its exact date is unresolved here; no securely dated earlier sequence/rank sense was established.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze inscription evidence; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use in this dossier, not proof that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.

senses.gloss: junior; younger person or lower in rank
senses.text: The character is also attested in senses involving junior status or sequence/rank, but the checked evidence does not establish when these uses began or whether one developed from the other.

senses.period: attestations cited from a Tang poem and later literature; witness dates not checked
senses.text: A literary use serves as humble self-reference among peers. Its precise mechanism and earliest occurrence are unresolved; it is not evidence that the character originally meant a first-person pronoun.
Classical citations are reported for female younger-sibling or junior use, but their manuscript dates and relationship to the broader junior sense are not established here.

senses.gloss: younger sibling; later narrowed in Japanese to younger male sibling
senses.period: Japanese oto use cited in 712; narrowing reported for the Edo period
senses.text: Japanese lexical history records oto for a younger person of either sex and reports a later narrowing of おとうと to a younger male sibling. This is the history of Japanese words, not evidence for the Chinese graph’s origin.

developments.text: The humble self-reference may relate pragmatically to a junior or younger-peer designation, but the evidence does not establish the pathway or its earliest use.

limitations.text: The binding-to-sequence explanation is an interpretation, and the dossier does not establish an independently dated sequence/rank use earlier than the sibling sense. No secure semantic chain between these senses can be given.
The dossier includes separate readings and senses, including an ethical 悌-related use, but does not establish a unified development joining them to the common sibling meaning.

overview.text: 弟 commonly means ‘younger brother’ and can also mean ‘junior.’ Its early form is interpreted as a binding around an implement, though the image and the route from it to the sibling sense are not firmly established.

components.text: Read the graph as one proposed picture of a binding wound around an implement; the implement’s identity and the image’s interpretation remain uncertain.

takeaway.text: The picture does not establish that ‘younger brother’ arose by sound borrowing: the depicted object’s name is unknown in the evidence.
